newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: C-C Amatil stake to be held for three years.
newsitem.headline: C-C Amatil stake to be held for three years.

text.p: San Miguel Corp of the Philippines has agreed to hold a 25 percent stake in Australian bottler Coca-Cola Amatil Ltd for three years, except in some limited circumstances, according to details of the link released on Tuesday.
The companies have also agreed not to compete in certain markets, while San Miguel will have a "top-up" right if its shareholding is reduced below 21 percent.
Under the share deal, signed last week, San Miguel will acquire a 25 percent stake in C-C Amatil in exchange for its soft-drink subsidiary Coca-Cola Bottler Philippines (CCBP).
The Coca-Cola Co, which owned 30 percent of CCPB, will also be issued shares in C-C Amatil, but its stake in the Australian group will be diluted from 36 percent to 33 percent.
The deal must be approved by C-C Amatil shareholders, who will vote at an extraordinary general meeting on July 1.
An independent expert's report by Grant Samuel & Co accompanying the notice of meeting, found the transaction was fair and reasonable to C-C Amatil shareholders.
Grant Samuel, which valued CCPB at A$3.3-A$3.9 billion, said the share issue valued the company at A$3.4 billion at C-C Amatil's average March 1997 share price of A$11.50.
C-C Amatil's share price has traded sharply higher since the deal was announced on April 3.

Grant Samuel said C-C Amatil's May 30 closing price of A$15.20 valued CCPB at A$4.45 billion, but did not believe this was an appropriate comparison as it reflected the market's recognition of the benefits of the tie-up.
"In any event, even if the consideration is valued at A$4.45 billion, CCA shareholders may still be better off if the proposed transaction proceeds than if it does not," the report said.
Grant Samuel said the acquisition of CCBP would significantly enhance C-C Amatil's earnings per share (EPS).
C-C Amatil's 1996 EPS would have risen 29.2 percent from 27.4 cents per share fully diluted to 35.4 cents per share if the deal had taken effect from January 1, 1996, it said.

Grant Samuel said this increase in pro forma EPS probably explained much of C-C Amatil's share price rise, but noted that C-C Amatil has invested in businesses that are expected to show more rapid earnings growth than CCBP.
"The effect of the acquisition of CCBP on CCA's EPS in the longer term is likely to be much less substantial as CCA's earnings grow," it said.
Grant Samuel said the deal would also reduce C-C Amatil's gearing, lead to operational benefits, and enhance the Australian group's prospects of becoming the key Coca-Cola bottler throughout Asia.
The disadvantages and risks of the deal were unlikely to be material, it said.
These included the fact that C-C Amatil would be more "controlled" with two major shareholders holding 58.4 percent of the company.
C-C Amatil would also be heavily exposed to the Philippine peso and Philippine country risks, while CCBP's market share and high profit margins could come under pressure.

San Miguel would also be issued 18 million share in C-C Amatil as part of "non-compete" agreements. Any attempt to sell these shares could put some downward pressure on C-C Amatil's share price, it said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
